Judging the Justification: Decision Certificate Supervision for
Generative Reward Models

Guiquan Sun Affiliation: School of Computing, University of Connecticut Email: guiquan.sun@uconn.edu    Bing Bai Affiliation: NEC Labs America Email: dongjin.song@uconn.edu    Martin Renqiang Min Affiliation: NEC Labs America Email: bbai@nec-labs.com    Dongjin Song ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: School of Computing, University of Connecticut Email: renqiang@nec-labs.com
Abstract

Generative reward models (GenRMs) generate natural language rationales to justify preference judgments, yet a correct verdict does not guarantee a sound justification. Existing approaches often rely on reference explanations to supervise rationales, but obtaining such references can be costly and does not necessarily establish whether generated rationales support the resulting verdict. To address these limitations, we propose DeCert (Decision-Certificate Supervision), a framework that evaluates the validity and verdict consistency of generated rationales without requiring reference explanations. Crucially, DeCert translates these assessments into preference supervision that accounts for both verdict correctness and justification quality. In particular, when multiple sampled judgments share the same correct verdict, differences in certificate quality enable DeCert to construct rationale preference pairs that distinguish stronger from weaker justifications. Extensive empirical studies across two model families and multiple in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that DeCert consistently outperforms strong generative judge baselines while improving rationale quality. Moreover, DeCert effectively mitigates positional bias, improving position-consistent accuracy by up to 14.8 points. These results highlight the importance of supervising not only which verdict is correct, but also how that verdict is justified. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/UConn-DSIS/DeCert.

1 Introduction

In pairwise evaluation, generative reward models (GenRMs) generate natural language rationales before selecting the preferred response, providing explicit justification for their judgments (Mahan et al., 2024). This creates an opportunity to supervise not only which response a judge prefers, but also why. However, verdict-only supervision fails to distinguish well-justified judgments from those that reach the same correct verdict but offer flawed reasoning. Recent findings highlight the importance of this distinction. For example, RationaleRM (Wang et al., 2026a) shows that reward models can achieve high accuracy on static preference benchmarks yet still generate flawed rationales and perform poorly when used to provide reward signals in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

Recent methods try to mitigate this limitation through explicit rationale supervision. For example, RationaleRM matches generated reasons to human atomic rationales, R-Align evaluates their logical alignment with human or synthesized reference explanations (Lai et al., 2026), and RM-NLHF extends critique-matching supervision to examples without human explanations through a learned MetaRM (Wang et al., 2026d). Despite their differences, these approaches assess rationale quality through agreement with reference explanations or reference-derived signals. Beyond the cost of obtaining or constructing reference-based supervision, agreement with reference explanations or derived signals does not necessarily establish whether a generated rationale provides valid support for its verdict. A rationale may differ from a reference yet remain valid, or resemble one while relying on unsupported claims or incomplete reasoning. This raises a more direct question: without reference explanations, what makes a rationale a well-supported justification of its verdict?

We formulate each judgment rationale as a decision certificate, i.e., a comparative argument intended to support its preference verdict. Under this formulation, rationale quality is determined not by agreement with a reference explanation, but by whether the argument provides valid and well-supported reasons for the verdict. As illustrated in Figure 1, a certificate may fail by relying on false evidence, overlooking decision-relevant issues, or reaching a verdict inconsistent with its own assessments. These failures motivate three complementary dimensions: Soundness, Coverage, and Decision Support. Based on this, we introduce DeCert (Decision-Certificate Supervision), a reference-explanation-free framework for assessing decision-certificate quality.

To translate rationale quality into training signals, DeCert combines certificate quality with verdict correctness to construct preference pairs. Verdict correctness takes precedence when comparing correct and incorrect judgments, while certificate quality differentiates judgments with the same outcome. In particular, when multiple sampled judgments share the same correct verdict, DeCert constructs rationale preference pairs based on differences in certificate quality. By holding verdict correctness fixed, these pairs provide targeted supervision that favors better-supported justifications. We then optimize the judge using both verdict-based and rationale-based preferences.

Extensive experiments across in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that DeCert outperforms strong generative judge baselines. Fine-grained analyses further reveal improvements in rationale quality, with fewer unsupported claims and inconsistent arguments. Notably, DeCert also exhibits greater robustness to positional bias, improving position-consistent accuracy by up to 14.814.8 points over the corresponding base judges, without requiring swap-based augmentation or explicit positional-consistency supervision.

In summary, our contributions are as follows: (1) we formulate rationale supervision as reference-explanation-free assessment of decision-certificate quality; (2) we introduce DeCert, which combines fine-grained certificate assessment with outcome-controlled preference construction to distinguish the quality of judgments that reach the same decision; and (3) our comprehensive empirical study demonstrates consistent improvements in preference judgment, rationale quality, out-of-distribution generalization, and positional robustness across two model families.

2 Related Work

Preference Learning and Reward Modeling. Learning from human preferences has been widely studied as a means of aligning model behavior with human judgments (Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022). Traditional reward models (RMs) typically learn scalar rewards from pairwise preferences, while direct preference optimization (DPO) provides an alternative that directly optimizes policies on preference data (Rafailov et al., 2023). The reliability of reward models is critical to preference alignment, motivating benchmarks such as RewardBench (Lambert et al., 2024) that examine their ability to distinguish responses across diverse tasks. While preference labels specify which response is preferred, they do not by themselves explain the evidence supporting that preference. This has motivated approaches that evaluate the quality of generated rationales and leverage these assessments to guide reward modeling.

LLM-as-a-Judge and Generative Reward Modeling. LLM-as-a-Judge methods leverage language models to evaluate open-ended responses, often generating natural language feedback or applying task-specific evaluation criteria (Zheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024a; Kim et al., 2024b; Shen et al., 2026). GenRMs further integrate reasoning and preference prediction, enabling judgments accompanied by explicit rationales (Mahan et al., 2024). Recent approaches improve these capabilities through reasoning distillation, reinforcement learning, or structured evaluation (Chen et al., 2026; Whitehouse et al., 2026; Saha et al., 2025). Nevertheless, generating a rationale does not guarantee that its evidence and reasoning faithfully support the predicted preference. Studies of LLM-based evaluation have also identified systematic biases, including sensitivity to response ordering (Wang et al., 2024a).

Rationale Supervision versus Process Reward Models. Process reward models (PRMs) supervise intermediate reasoning steps in a solver’s solution process to improve reasoning correctness (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b). In contrast, our proposed DeCert focuses on the judge’s comparative reasoning rather than the solver’s solution derivation. Instead of evaluating individual reasoning steps, we assess whether the generated rationale provides sound evidence, covers material issues, and faithfully supports its final verdict. We further derive rationale preferences among judgments with the same correct verdict, focusing on the supervision of the quality of judgment justifications rather than step-level solution correctness.

Rationale Supervision for Generative Judges. Recent studies have explored supervising judgment rationales through reference explanations or human critiques (Wang et al., 2026a; Lai et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026e), as well as self-generated critiques, evaluation criteria, and analysis preferences (Yu et al., 2025a; Liang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2026). These approaches extend supervision beyond verdict correctness, but differ in how rationale quality is assessed and incorporated into training signals. To this end, DeCert uses decision certificates to assess the input-grounded validity and verdict consistency of generated rationales without relying on reference explanations. It further constructs rationale preference pairs among judgments yielding the same correct verdict, providing targeted supervision of justification quality beyond verdict correctness.

3 Decision-Certificate Supervision

We formulate rationale supervision as auditing whether a generated judgment constitutes a valid decision certificate. Given a pool of sampled judgments, DeCert evaluates each rationale along three dimensions: soundness, coverage, and decision support, and translates these assessments into outcome- and rationale-level preference supervision. Figure 2 gives an overview.

3.1 Problem Formulation

Pairwise judgment. Let ξ=(x,yA,yB,𝒫)\xi=(x,y_{A},y_{B},\mathcal{P}) denote a pairwise evaluation instance, where xx is the request, yAy_{A} and yBy_{B} are candidate responses, and 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a prespecified evaluation policy. A generative judge πθ\pi_{\theta} produces

J=(r,v)∼πθ(⋅∣ξ),J=(r,v)\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\xi),

where rr is a natural language rationale and v∈{−1,+1}v\in\{-1,+1\} denotes selecting BB or AA, respectively. Each training instance provides a reference preference v⋆v^{\star}, but no reference rationale.

Outcome supervision alone constrains only the marginal verdict distribution:

ℛout​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{out}}(\theta) =𝔼(ξ,v⋆)𝔼(r,v)∼πθ(⋅∣ξ)𝟏[v=v⋆]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(\xi,v^{\star})}\mathbb{E}_{(r,v)\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\xi)}\mathbf{1}[v=v^{\star}] (1)
=𝔼(ξ,v⋆)​πθ​(v⋆∣ξ).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(\xi,v^{\star})}\pi_{\theta}(v^{\star}\mid\xi).

Thus, judges with the same probability of predicting the correct verdict can receive the same outcome reward while inducing substantially different conditional rationale distributions πθ​(r∣ξ,v⋆)\pi_{\theta}(r\mid\xi,v^{\star}). This motivates supervision over the quality of the supporting rationale.

Evaluation policy. Let 𝒦⁡(ξ)\mathcal{K}(\xi) denote the applicable criteria for an instance. The policy specifies criterion importance weights αk>0\alpha_{k}>0, which we normalize as

ωk=αk∑ℓ∈𝒦⁡(ξ)αℓ.\omega_{k}=\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{K}(\xi)}\alpha_{\ell}}. (2)

For a criterion-level preference vector 𝒅=(dk)k∈𝒦⁡(ξ)\boldsymbol{d}=(d_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}(\xi)}, with dk∈[−1,1]d_{k}\in[-1,1] and positive values favoring AA, the policy aggregates criterion-level comparisons as

F𝒫​(𝒅)=∑k∈𝒦⁡(ξ)ωk​dk.F_{\mathcal{P}}(\boldsymbol{d})=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(\xi)}\omega_{k}d_{k}. (3)

3.2 Decision-Certificate Assessment

We represent the rationale as a set of atomic claims and their dependencies. Let 𝒢r=(𝒜r,ℰr)\mathcal{G}_{r}=(\mathcal{A}_{r},\mathcal{E}_{r}) be a directed acyclic graph extracted from rr, where each node aj∈𝒜ra_{j}\in\mathcal{A}_{r} is

aj=(tj,kj,pj,ej,pa⁡(j)).a_{j}=(t_{j},k_{j},p_{j},e_{j},\operatorname{pa}(j)). (4)

Here, tjt_{j} denotes the claim type, kjk_{j} its associated evaluation criterion, pjp_{j} the atomic proposition, eje_{j} the cited evidence when applicable, and pa⁡(j)\operatorname{pa}(j) its parent claims. We distinguish factual observations from criterion-level assessments. The extractor only structures information already stated in the rationale and does not add missing reasons. Details are provided in Appendix A.

Soundness. Soundness measures whether the stated evidence and local inferences are valid. We use a natural language inference verifier for two local checks. For each claim aja_{j}, gj∈[0,1]g_{j}\in[0,1] measures whether its factual content is supported by the cited evidence, while ℓj∈[0,1]\ell_{j}\in[0,1] measures whether its conclusion follows from its parent claims:

νj=gj​ℓj.\nu_{j}=g_{j}\ell_{j}. (5)

For a leaf observation, we set ℓj=1\ell_{j}=1; for a purely inferential node without an additional external factual claim, we set gj=1g_{j}=1. We provide implementation details in Appendix A.

Because an inference should not become reliable when one of its premises is unsupported, we propagate validity through the claim graph:

qj=minh∈Anc+⁡(j)⁡νh,q_{j}=\min_{h\in\operatorname{Anc}^{+}(j)}\nu_{h}, (6)

where Anc+⁡(j)\operatorname{Anc}^{+}(j) contains aja_{j} and all of its ancestors. Let 𝒜r,k\mathcal{A}_{r,k} denote the substantive claims associated with criterion kk after semantic deduplication. We define

sk={minaj∈𝒜r,k⁡qj,𝒜r,k≠∅,1,𝒜r,k=∅,​Ssnd​(J)=∏k∈𝒦⁡(ξ)skωk.s_{k}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\min_{a_{j}\in\mathcal{A}_{r,k}}q_{j},&\mathcal{A}_{r,k}\neq\varnothing,\\[4.0pt] 1,&\mathcal{A}_{r,k}=\varnothing,\end{cases}S_{\mathrm{snd}}(J)=\prod_{k\in\mathcal{K}(\xi)}s_{k}^{\omega_{k}}. (7)

Coverage. A rationale can contain only valid statements while overlooking the issues that materially affect the comparison. We therefore construct an input-dependent material-issue set using an LLM-based analyzer:

Dξ=𝒜ϕ​(ξ)={(dt,kt,ρt)}t=1M,ρt>0.D_{\xi}=\mathcal{A}_{\phi}(\xi)=\{(d_{t},k_{t},\rho_{t})\}_{t=1}^{M},\qquad\rho_{t}>0. (8)

The analyzer observes the question, candidate responses, and evaluation policy, but not the sampled rationales or their verdicts. Each dtd_{t} describes an important requirement, error, or response difference, ktk_{t} identifies its criterion, and ρt\rho_{t} represents its importance. Let mt​j∈[0,1]m_{tj}\in[0,1] measure how well claim aja_{j} addresses material issue dtd_{t}. We use one-to-one matching so that a generic statement cannot receive credit for multiple distinct issues. We represent a partial one-to-one matching by P∈{0,1}M×|𝒜r|P\in\{0,1\}^{M\times|\mathcal{A}_{r}|}, where Pt​j=1P_{tj}=1 indicates that issue dtd_{t} is matched to claim aja_{j}. Coverage is then

Scov​(J)=max⁡∑t,jP∈ℳ⁡ρt​Pt​j​mt​j​qj∑tρt.S_{\mathrm{cov}}(J)=\frac{\displaystyle\max_{P\in\mathcal{M}}\sum_{t,j}\rho_{t}P_{tj}m_{tj}q_{j}}{\displaystyle\sum_{t}\rho_{t}}. (9)

Multiplying by qjq_{j} prevents an unsupported claim from receiving full coverage credit. Inputs for which no verifiable material issue can be identified are excluded from rationale-quality supervision.

Decision Support. Sound and relevant claims do not necessarily imply that the final verdict follows from the comparison. We therefore ask whether the verified information is sufficient to support vv under the evaluation policy.

For each criterion kk, verified criterion-level assessments induce an interval

Ik​(r)=[Lk,Uk]⊆[−1,1]I_{k}(r)=[L_{k},U_{k}]\subseteq[-1,1] (10)

for its comparison value dkd_{k}. An explicitly supported tie yields Ik​(r)={0}I_{k}(r)=\{0\}. We detail interval construction in Appendix A.3.

The rationale therefore defines the feasible comparison set

Ωr=∏k∈𝒦⁡(ξ)Ik​(r).\Omega_{r}=\prod_{k\in\mathcal{K}(\xi)}I_{k}(r). (11)

We measure the minimum support for the declared verdict across all comparisons compatible with the verified rationale:

Br​(v)\displaystyle B_{r}(v) =inf𝒅∈Ωrv​F𝒫​(𝒅)\displaystyle=\inf_{\boldsymbol{d}\in\Omega_{r}}vF_{\mathcal{P}}(\boldsymbol{d}) (12)
=v​∑kωk​Lk+Uk2−∑kωk​Uk−Lk2,\displaystyle=v\sum_{k}\omega_{k}\frac{L_{k}+U_{k}}{2}-\sum_{k}\omega_{k}\frac{U_{k}-L_{k}}{2},
Sdec​(J)\displaystyle S_{\mathrm{dec}}(J) =1+Br​(v)2.\displaystyle=\frac{1+B_{r}(v)}{2}.

Because Br​(v)∈[−1,1]B_{r}(v)\in[-1,1], Sdec∈[0,1]S_{\mathrm{dec}}\in[0,1]. In particular, Br​(v)>0B_{r}(v)>0 means that every criterion configuration consistent with the verified rationale supports the stated verdict. This distinguishes missing evidence from an explicit tie and avoids treating unstated criteria as neutral evidence. We provide detailed derivations in the appendix A.4.

Overall certificate quality. We combine the three dimensions using the geometric mean:

Qproc​(J)=(Ssnd​(J)​Scov​(J)​Sdec​(J))1/3.Q_{\mathrm{proc}}(J)=\left(S_{\mathrm{snd}}(J)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(J)S_{\mathrm{dec}}(J)\right)^{1/3}. (13)

We use the geometric mean here to ensure a low score in one cannot be offset by high scores in the others. Appendix C.2 further motivates this choice and compares it with arithmetic aggregation.

3.3 Preference Data Construction

Candidate generation. For each training sample, we construct a candidate pool 𝒥⁡(ξ)\mathcal{J}(\xi) by sampling 33 judgments from GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) and 55 from Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025). Each judgment J=(r,v)J=(r,v) is assigned a rationale quality score Qproc​(J)Q_{\mathrm{proc}}(J) and an outcome score O(J)=𝟏[v=v⋆]O(J)=\mathbf{1}[v=v^{\star}]. To combine both, we define a total score of a judgment:

Qtotal​(J)=O⁡(J)+λ​Qproc​(J)1+λ,0<λ<1.Q_{\mathrm{total}}(J)=\frac{O(J)+\lambda Q_{\mathrm{proc}}(J)}{1+\lambda},0<\lambda<1. (14)

Then we use this to rank candidates. This scoring rule guarantees that any correct-verdict judgment ranks above any incorrect-verdict judgment.

General preference pairs. For pools containing both correct and incorrect verdicts, we select the highest- and lowest-scoring candidates under QtotalQ_{\mathrm{total}} as (J+,J−)(J^{+},J^{-}). The highest-scoring candidates are also used as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) samples for warm-up.

Rationale preference pairs. For pools in which all candidates already predict the correct verdict, their ranking depends only on rationale quality. We therefore select the candidates with the highest and lowest QprocQ_{\mathrm{proc}} scores and retain the pair if

Qproc​(J+)−Qproc​(J−)>δ.Q_{\mathrm{proc}}(J^{+})-Q_{\mathrm{proc}}(J^{-})>\delta. (15)

Where δ\delta is the score gap threshold. We further compare different choices of the threshold in Appendix C.1. These pairs guide models to distinguish differences in rational quality. Pools containing only incorrect verdicts are discarded.

Two-Stage Alignment. For training, we adopt SFT (Wei et al., 2021) and DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) due to their efficiency and lower computational cost. We use Llama3.1-8B (AI, 2024) and Qwen3-8B as base models and follow a two-stage training pipeline with SFT followed by DPO. We apply Low-Rank Adaptation (Hu et al., 2022) for computational efficiency. Further configuration details are provided in Appendix B.2.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experiments Setup

Training data and models. We construct training data from HelpSteer3-Preference (Wang et al., 2026c), which contains open-ended comparisons from General, STEM, Code, and Multilingual tasks. We first sample around 12k instances, balanced across four domains. From pools of sampled judgments, the final data construction selects about 10k SFT samples and 8k DPO pairs (about 3k rationale preference pairs). We train two base models from different model families. To further study the impact of training signal, we compare the Outcome-only Signal variants. Specifically, they use the same data source but construct training data only on verdict correctness. Additional construction and optimization details are in Appendix B.

Evaluation data and metrics. We evaluate on the test set of HelpSteer3 (2k). We also use two out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks, i.e., RM-Bench (Liu et al., 2024) which measures a model’s ability to discriminate subtle differences and style biases across Chat, Code, Math, and Safety, and JudgeBench (Tan et al., 2025) which emphasizes deep judgment and logical reasoning on challenging Knowledge and Reasoning tasks. For HelpSteer3, Acc. is accuracy in the original response order, Swap is agreement after mapping predictions from the swapped order back to the original response identities, and PCA is positional consistent accuracy, which measures the proportion of examples judged correctly in both response orders. Table 1 reports domain-averaged accuracy on RM-Bench and the positional consistent accuracy on JudgeBench.

Baselines. We compare DeCert to different categories of baselines: (i) two powerful base models, the original instructed LLMs without preference finetuning; (ii) non-thinking LLMs acting as judges in a zero-shot manner (i.e., GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024), Claude-3.5-Sonnet (Anthropic, 2024)); (iii) state-of-the-art generative reward models that belong to the same category as DeCert (i.e., J1-Llama-8B (Whitehouse et al., 2026), R-Align-8B (Lai et al., 2026), Con-J-7B (Ye et al., 2025), RewardAnything-8B (Yu et al., 2025b), GRAM-R2R^{2} (Wang et al., 2026b)) and thinking LLMs acting as judges (i.e., Nemotron-30B-A3B (Chandiramani et al., 2026)). Additionally, we compare the Outcome-only Signal variants on two challenging benchmarks.

4.2 Overall Judgment Performance

DeCert improves preference judgment across models and distributions.

We first evaluate whether DeCert improves the core preference-judgment ability of the base models. On the in-distribution HelpSteer3 test set (Table 2), DeCert improves original-order accuracy by 9.1 points for Llama-3.1-8B and 6.3 points for Qwen3-8B over their corresponding base judges (p<0.0001p<0.0001).

The improvements transfer to OOD evaluation in Table 1. Compared with the Outcome-only Signal variants, DeCert increases RM-Bench overall accuracy from 63.3 to 67.0 for Llama and from 73.5 to 76.2 for Qwen. On JudgeBench, positional consistent accuracy increases from 39.1 to 42.6 and from 48.3 to 52.0, respectively. Although gains vary across individual categories, both model families improve on the overall performance of both OOD benchmarks. Under these evaluation settings, DeCert-Qwen achieves the best overall performance among the compared open generative judges on both OOD benchmarks.

4.3 What Does Rationale Supervision Add?

All-correct judgments provide supervision beyond outcome labels.

Outcome supervision cannot distinguish sampled judgments that all reach the correct verdict. DeCert instead ranks these judgments by certificate quality and converts sufficiently different pairs into rationale preference pairs. Figure 3 isolates the contribution of these all-correct examples. Adding rationale preference pairs increases PCA from 46.7% to 52.9% on RM-Bench and from 39.1% to 42.6% on JudgeBench, corresponding to gains of 6.2 and 3.5 points. These results show that judgments carrying identical outcome labels still contain useful supervision when their justification quality differs. Besides, we provide a more comprehensive ablation in Appendix C.3.

The additional supervision transfers to rationale quality metrics.

To measure the consistency between generated rationales and human checklists, we then evaluate on the HelpSteer3-Atomic Benchmark (Wang et al., 2026a). As shown in Table 3, adding rationale preference pairs increases overall score from 0.2212 to 0.2624 and multilingual score from 0.2973 to 0.3589. Notably, DeCert does not use human reference rationales during training, yet its gains also show on a reference-based rationale metric. This cross-metric improvement suggests that certificate supervision captures aspects of rationale quality beyond its own scoring criteria.

4.4 Rationale Quality and Evidence Sensitivity

DeCert reduces common rationale flaws.

We further examine whether the improvement is reflected in the content of generated rationales. Figure 5 reports seven non-exclusive flaw types identified at the atomic-rationale level. DeCert reduces the observed rate of every flaw type. The largest reduction occurs for non sequiturs, which decrease from 21.5% to 3.3%. Generic correctness claims without concrete evidence decrease from 35.0% to 25.1%, while single-sided praise decreases from 3.6% to 1.7%. Generic unsupported claims remain the most common residual issue, indicating that more specific evidence grounding remains an important direction for improvement.

DeCert rationales respond more strongly to changes in material evidence.

Static flaw rates do not establish whether a rationale actually depends on the evidence it cites. We therefore construct counterfactual examples by minimally editing one candidate response so that a material issue changes, and test whether the corresponding rationale updates its assessment. Figure 4 reports results on 1k edited pairs. DeCert increases Evidence Adaptation Rate (EAR) from 64.5% to 88.9% and reduces Stale Rationale Rate (SRR) from 34.0% to 11.1%. Qwen shows the same pattern: EAR increases from 87.2% to 93.4%, while SRR decreases from 30.5% to 7.3%. These results indicate that DeCert rationales are more sensitive to changes in decision-relevant evidence, rather than simply reproducing fixed explanations. We also provide a case study in Appendix E.

4.5 Positional Robustness

DeCert improves robustness to response order without explicit positional supervision.

Finally, we test whether DeCert is robust to changes in response order. On HelpSteer3, DeCert improves swap agreement by 13.0 points for Llama and 13.5 points for Qwen relative to the corresponding base judges. Positional consistent accuracy improves by 14.8 and 9.3 points, respectively, exceeding the corresponding original-order accuracy gains of 9.1 and 6.3 points. Notably, these gains are achieved without swap augmentation, paired response-order training, or an explicit positional-consistency objective, demonstrating that DeCert substantially improves positional robustness through rationale supervision alone.

5 Conclusion

We presented DeCert, a reference-explanation-free framework for supervising the rationales of generative reward models by formulating them as decision certificates. Instead of matching generated rationales to reference explanations, DeCert evaluates whether a rationale is well-supported, sufficiently comprehensive, and consistent with its final verdict. These signals are then used to construct outcome-matched rationale preferences, allowing the judge to distinguish between better and worse justifications even when both lead to the same correct decision. Across two model families and multiple in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks, DeCert consistently improves both preference judgment and rationale quality over outcome-only supervision. Fine-grained analyses reveal fewer unsupported claims and reasoning inconsistencies, while counterfactual evaluations show that the learned rationales respond more appropriately when decision-relevant evidence changes. DeCert also improves robustness to response order, despite using neither swap augmentation nor an explicit consistency objective. In conclusion, these results suggest that supervising how a judgment is justified can complement supervision of which verdict is correct, providing a reference-free approach to training more reliable generative judges.

6 Limitations

DeCert has several limitations. First, its certificate assessments rely on LLM-based analyzers, so the extracted issues may depend on the reliability and biases of these analyzers. Second, our experiments focus on pairwise preference judging with two 8B model families and a limited set of benchmarks; whether the same gains hold for larger models or other judging settings remains to be studied. Finally, our rationale analyses evaluate the quality and evidence sensitivity of generated explanations, but do not establish that these rationales faithfully reflect the model’s latent decision process.

Appendix A Implementation Details of DeCert

A.1 Evaluation Policies

We use an LLM to generate domain-specific rubrics for the evaluation. Table 4 lists the domain-specific criterion weights used in our implementation. Omitted criteria are excluded from score aggregation.

We parse each judgment into criterion-level observations, inferences, and winners, together with a final verdict. A judgment is considered parseable if it contains at least one criterion block with a valid <result> field and an <answer> selecting AA or BB. Unparseable judgments receive zero scores and are excluded from preference-pair construction.

A.2 Material-Issue Extraction and Matching

The material-issue analyzer receives the evaluation input ξ=(x,yA,yB,𝒫)\xi=(x,y_{A},y_{B},\mathcal{P}) without access to any sampled rationale or verdict, and extracts at most six material issues:

Dξ={dt=(ut,kt,ρt,st)}t=1M,D_{\xi}=\{d_{t}=(u_{t},k_{t},\rho_{t},s_{t})\}_{t=1}^{M}, (16)

where utu_{t} describes the issue, ktk_{t} denotes the associated evaluation criterion, ρt∈[1,3]\rho_{t}\in[1,3] its importance, and st∈{−1,0,+1}s_{t}\in\{-1,0,+1\} its comparison direction.

For each material issue dtd_{t} and rationale claim aja_{j}, we compute a matching score mt​j∈{0,0.5,1}m_{tj}\in\{0,0.5,1\} according to whether the claim correctly addresses the same issue with a compatible assessment direction. Free-form summary statements are excluded from matching.

Let Nr=|𝒜r|N_{r}=|\mathcal{A}_{r}|. We use the maximum-weight partial one-to-one matching {P∈{0,1}M×|𝒜r|}\{P\in\{0,1\}^{M\times|\mathcal{A}_{r}|}\}, with pairwise weight

wt​j=ρt​mt​j​qj,w_{tj}=\rho_{t}\,m_{tj}\,q_{j}, (17)

where qjq_{j} is the verified support-chain validity of claim aja_{j}. The resulting coverage score follows Eq. 9.

If the analyzer identifies no verifiable material issue (M=0M=0), the instance is excluded from training rather than assigned a default coverage score.

A.3 Constructing Criterion Intervals from Verified Conclusions

For each criterion kk, the comparison scale and admissible forms of criterion-level conclusions are specified before auditing. We normalize the scale to 𝒵k⊆[−1,1]\mathcal{Z}_{k}\subseteq[-1,1], where larger values favor AA. A simple choice is

𝒵k={−1,0,+1},\mathcal{Z}_{k}=\{-1,0,+1\},

representing that BB is better, the two responses are tied, or AA is better, respectively. A finer finite scale may be used when the evaluation policy provides explicit comparison rules.

Let ℋk​(r)\mathcal{H}_{k}(r) denote the set of verified comparative predicates for criterion kk that are explicitly stated in rationale rr. We include a predicate only when its supporting claim chain satisfies the local-validity threshold τloc\tau_{\mathrm{loc}}. Typical predicates include dk≥bd_{k}\geq b, dk≤bd_{k}\leq b, and dk=bd_{k}=b, where b∈𝒵kb\in\mathcal{Z}_{k}. Each predicate retains the claims and evidence from which it was derived. The values compatible with these verified predicates are

ℬk​(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{k}(r) ={z∈𝒵k:ψ⁡(z)​ holds for every ​ψ∈ℋk​(r)},\displaystyle=\left\{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{k}:\psi(z)\text{ holds for every }\psi\in\mathcal{H}_{k}(r)\right\}, (18)
Ik​(r)\displaystyle I_{k}(r) =[min⁡ℬk​(r),max⁡ℬk​(r)].\displaystyle=\left[\min\mathcal{B}_{k}(r),\max\mathcal{B}_{k}(r)\right].

Thus, Ik​(r)I_{k}(r) is the interval hull of the admissible criterion values. Using the interval hull provides a conservative outer approximation when 𝒵k\mathcal{Z}_{k} is discrete.

If ℋk​(r)=∅\mathcal{H}_{k}(r)=\varnothing, no verified comparative information is available for criterion kk, and we retain the full interval Ik​(r)=[−1,1]I_{k}(r)=[-1,1]. If ℬk​(r)=∅\mathcal{B}_{k}(r)=\varnothing, the accepted predicates are mutually inconsistent; we therefore reject the corresponding certificate. Unparseable dependency graphs, cyclic dependencies, or missing verification records are handled similarly.

Importantly, verifying a local error does not by itself establish a complete criterion-level comparison. For example, confirming an error in yAy_{A} does not imply that yBy_{B} is better on criterion kk unless the evidence and the prespecified evaluation rule jointly support that conclusion. We therefore narrow Ik​(r)I_{k}(r) only when a verified comparative predicate constrains the relative criterion value dkd_{k}. The resulting intervals summarize conclusions supported by the audited rationale; they should not be interpreted as statistical confidence or credible intervals. Their validity depends on the reliability of the underlying grounding and inference checks.

A.4 Closed-Form Conservative Decision Margin

For each criterion, let

mk=Lk+Uk2,hk=Uk−Lk2.m_{k}=\frac{L_{k}+U_{k}}{2},\qquad h_{k}=\frac{U_{k}-L_{k}}{2}.

Every dk∈[Lk,Uk]d_{k}\in[L_{k},U_{k}] can be written as

dk=mk+hk​ηk,ηk∈[−1,1].d_{k}=m_{k}+h_{k}\eta_{k},\qquad\eta_{k}\in[-1,1].

Recall that the policy score is

F𝒫​(𝒅)=∑kωk​dk,F_{\mathcal{P}}(\boldsymbol{d})=\sum_{k}\omega_{k}d_{k},

where ωk≥0\omega_{k}\geq 0 and ∑kωk=1\sum_{k}\omega_{k}=1. For a declared verdict v∈{−1,+1}v\in\{-1,+1\},

inf𝒅∈Ωrv​F𝒫​(𝒅)\displaystyle\inf_{\boldsymbol{d}\in\Omega_{r}}vF_{\mathcal{P}}(\boldsymbol{d}) =inf𝜼∈[−1,1]|𝒦⁡(ξ)|v​∑kωk​(mk+hk​ηk)\displaystyle=\inf_{\boldsymbol{\eta}\in[-1,1]^{|\mathcal{K}(\xi)|}}v\sum_{k}\omega_{k}(m_{k}+h_{k}\eta_{k}) (19)
=v​∑kωk​mk+∑kinfηk∈[−1,1]v​ωk​hk​ηk\displaystyle=v\sum_{k}\omega_{k}m_{k}+\sum_{k}\inf_{\eta_{k}\in[-1,1]}v\omega_{k}h_{k}\eta_{k}
=v​∑kωk​mk−∑kωk​hk.\displaystyle=v\sum_{k}\omega_{k}m_{k}-\sum_{k}\omega_{k}h_{k}.

This yields the closed form used in Eq. (12):

Br​(v)=v​∑kωk​Lk+Uk2−∑kωk​Uk−Lk2.B_{r}(v)=v\sum_{k}\omega_{k}\frac{L_{k}+U_{k}}{2}-\sum_{k}\omega_{k}\frac{U_{k}-L_{k}}{2}. (20)

The first term is the signed policy score at the center of the feasible region, while the second term subtracts the total unresolved uncertainty. Consequently, wider unresolved intervals reduce the support margin even when the currently verified evidence favors the declared verdict.

Two special cases illustrate this behavior. If every criterion is fixed to a verified point value, then Lk=Uk=dkL_{k}=U_{k}=d_{k} and hk=0h_{k}=0, giving

Br​(v)=v​∑kωk​dk.B_{r}(v)=v\sum_{k}\omega_{k}d_{k}. (21)

Thus, the conservative margin reduces to the ordinary signed policy score.

Alternatively, suppose only a subset 𝒱⊆𝒦⁡(ξ)\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{K}(\xi) has verified point values, while all remaining criteria are unresolved with Ik​(r)=[−1,1]I_{k}(r)=[-1,1]. Then

Br​(v)=v​∑k∈𝒱ωk​dk−∑k∉𝒱ωk.B_{r}(v)=v\sum_{k\in\mathcal{V}}\omega_{k}d_{k}-\sum_{k\notin\mathcal{V}}\omega_{k}. (22)

Hence, unresolved criteria retain their policy weight as potential evidence against the declared verdict rather than disappearing through renormalization over the criteria already discussed by the rationale. To study the effect of score aggregation, we construct preference data by using two different ways on the same data source. Table 7 shows that geometric aggregation achieves better performance on two challenging benchmarks.

Appendix B Experiments Details

B.1 Training Objectives

We first formulate the training objectives in two stages. SFT (Wei et al., 2021) minimizes the negative log-likelihood of selected judgments:

ℒSFT​(θ)=−𝔼(ξ,J)∼𝒟SFT​[log⁡πθ​(J∣ξ)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(\xi,J)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SFT}}}[\log\pi_{\theta}(J\mid\xi)]. (23)

The judge is then initialized from the SFT checkpoint and optimized using the standard DPO loss (Rafailov et al., 2023):

ℒDPO(θ)=−𝔼(ξ,J+,J−)∼𝒟DPO[\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(\xi,J^{+},J^{-})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{DPO}}}\Bigg[ log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(J+∣ξ)πref​(J+∣ξ)CLOSE\displaystyle\log\sigma\Bigg(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(J^{+}\mid\xi)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(J^{+}\mid\xi)} (24)
−βlogπθ​(J−∣ξ)πref​(J−∣ξ))],\displaystyle-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(J^{-}\mid\xi)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(J^{-}\mid\xi)}\Bigg)\Bigg],

where πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is the reference policy and β\beta is the DPO temperature parameter.

For DPO pair construction, we use λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 to calculate total scores. Groups whose parseable judgments are all incorrect are discarded.

B.2 Training Parameter

For all training conducted in this paper, we adopt Low-Rank Adaptation (Hu et al., 2022) for efficiency. All training was conducted using four A100-40GB GPUs or L40 GPUs.

SFT Training. For all supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we use a batch size of 1 per device with gradient accumulation over 16 steps. Training employs a linear learning-rate scheduler with an initial learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} and a warmup ratio of 0.05. To improve stability, we enable gradient checkpointing to reduce memory overhead. Optimization is performed with RMSprop, and trained with 1 epoch.

DPO Training. For direct preference optimization (DPO), training is conducted for 3 epochs with a batch size of 1 per device and gradient accumulation over 16 steps. The learning rate remains 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, but we switch to a cosine scheduler for smoother convergence. We continue to apply gradient checkpointing. To regulate policy updates, we set the DPO regularization parameter β=0.1\beta=0.1, ensuring stability while maintaining alignment with human preferences.

B.3 Model Checkpoints and Decoding

Table 5 gives the exact public checkpoints used for our local evaluation and the corresponding decoding temperatures.

Appendix C Extended Experiment Results

C.1 Comparison of Different Rationale Score Thresholds

We conduct additional experiments on the benchmarks as in the main experiments to compare different thresholds for rationale score gap, including δ={0.15,0.2,0.25}\delta=\{0.15,0.2,0.25\}. The δ\delta is set to 0.25 by default. As shown in Table 6, the model shows a slight improvement, but the benefit here is limited because, as the threshold increases, the filtered data also decreases.

C.2 Comparison of Different Score Aggregation Strategies

The scoring hierarchy uses different aggregation rules for different relationships. Across certificate dimensions, a geometric mean discourages compensation for a failed requirement. For comparison, the arithmetic alternative is

Qprocarith​(J)=Ssnd​(J)+Scov​(J)+Sdec​(J)3.Q_{\mathrm{proc}}^{\mathrm{arith}}(J)=\frac{S_{\mathrm{snd}}(J)+S_{\mathrm{cov}}(J)+S_{\mathrm{dec}}(J)}{3}. (25)

For example, scores (1,1,0)(1,1,0) yield 2/32/3 under the arithmetic mean but 00 under the geometric mean. The aggregation ablation evaluates this choice empirically. We use the arithmetic alternative to aggregate the total score for preference data construction. The experiment results are shown in Table 7. Based on the results, the geometric mean achieves better performance than the arithmetic mean on two benchmarks, which shows the effectiveness of the geometric mean aggregation.

C.3 Ablation of Rationale Scoring

We examine how the three rationale scores respond to different certificate flaws and how their aggregation affects sensitivity to these flaws. Using the same original and perturbed judgments, we compare SsndS_{\mathrm{snd}}, ScovS_{\mathrm{cov}}, and SdecS_{\mathrm{dec}} individually, as well as their geometric mean Qgeo=QprocQ_{\mathrm{geo}}=Q_{\mathrm{proc}} and arithmetic mean QarithQ_{\mathrm{arith}}.

Setup.

We apply five types of controlled edits to 2k original judgments. Two are intended to preserve rationale validity: valid trade-off (VT) adds a truthful secondary advantage of the non-preferred response, and irrelevant true details (ITD) adds true observations that are irrelevant to the preference decision. Three edits introduce flaws: fabricated evidence (FE) replaces supporting observations with invented details while preserving the criterion conclusions and verdict; missing key issues (MKI) removes verdict-supporting criterion blocks; and reversed verdict (RV) flips the final verdict while keeping the rationale unchanged.

Evaluation protocol.

For each score ss, we compute the paired change Δs=s⁡(J′)−s⁡(J)\Delta_{s}=s(J^{\prime})-s(J), where JJ and J′J^{\prime} are the original and perturbed judgments. We count a harmful edit as detected when Δs<−τ\Delta_{s}<-\tau, with τ=0.05\tau=0.05. For VT and ITD, success instead requires Δs≥−τ\Delta_{s}\geq-\tau, so a larger score decrease is a false positive. Figure 6 reports these success rates, equivalent to one minus the corresponding miss or false-positive rate. The detection threshold τ\tau is distinct from the score-gap threshold δ\delta used to select rationale preference pairs during training.

Individual scores.

Figure 6(a) shows that the components respond to different flaws. Soundness detects 90.5% of FE edits, but only 30.4% of MKI and 1.0% of RV edits. Coverage achieves the highest MKI detection rate among the individual scores (64.1%), but detects only 24.0% of FE and 7.0% of RV edits. Decision support detects 95.5% of reversed verdicts, while detecting only 19.5% of FE and 47.8% of MKI edits. These results support treating the three dimensions as complementary checks: a rationale can contain grounded claims yet omit material support, or cover relevant issues yet draw an inconsistent verdict.

Aggregation.

In Figure 6(b), geometric aggregation achieves detection rates of 89.5%, 67.4%, and 92.0% on FE, MKI, and RV, respectively, compared with 86.5%, 62.5%, and 90.0% for arithmetic aggregation. This pattern is consistent with the geometric mean reducing compensation for a low component score by higher scores in other dimensions. The improvement comes with a modest increase in false positives: success rates on VT and ITD are 83.5% and 79.5% for the geometric mean, compared with 86.0% and 81.5% for the arithmetic mean. Geometric aggregation therefore provides greater sensitivity to the tested harmful edits, with a small cost in tolerance of the intended non-corrupting edits. MKI remains the hardest harmful perturbation for the combined score, indicating that detecting omitted support remains an area for improvement.

Appendix D Deployment of Analyzer

Advanced proprietary models require costly API calls during data construction. We therefore compare paid and open-source models as the material-issue analyzer. Specifically, we measure the alignment between material issues extracted by different models and reference issues on 500 human-annotated data. As shown in Table 8, GPT-4o-mini achieves nearly the same recall as GPT-4o while costing approximately 16.7×16.7\times less per token. The locally hosted Qwen3-8B also remains competitive: its F1 decreases by only 4.6 % and its precision is nearly unchanged. These results show that lower-cost or open-source models can provide a practical approximation when using frontier models like GPT-4o is not affordable. In this work, we adopted GPT-4o-mini as the analyzer for issue extraction, considering its balance between effectiveness and computational efficiency.

Appendix E Case Study: Same Verdict, Different Rationale Quality

Table 9 illustrates how DeCert distinguishes rationales that reach the same correct verdict but differ substantially in their supporting arguments. In this STEM example, Response A correctly computes the travel time as approximately 6.626.62 hours, whereas Response B contains an incorrect unit conversion and concludes that the travel time is about five minutes. Both sampled judgments correctly prefer Response A.

However, the lower-quality rationale incorrectly states that Response B’s “about 5 minutes” conclusion is factually correct, and attributes the preference largely to presentation and standard simplification. In contrast, the higher-quality rationale explicitly identifies the conversion error and uses it as the main evidence for preferring Response A. Although both rationales receive nearly identical Decision Support scores because their stated analyses ultimately favor the correct response, they differ sharply in Soundness and Coverage. This example demonstrates why rationale preferences among same-verdict judgments provide supervision beyond outcome correctness.

Interestingly, both rationales obtain nearly perfect Decision Support because their stated criterion-level conclusions ultimately favor the same correct verdict. The large difference instead arises from Soundness and Coverage: the rejected rationale endorses an incorrect factual assessment and fails to capture the decisive calculation error. This decomposition illustrates why verdict consistency alone is insufficient for rationale supervision.
